entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The milky sap of the mukuyu tree, used as a glue in making arrows of reeds
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Derived from Ku vala, Valavala, with a reduplication of the first syllable
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.n.]

entries.english: A comb made of wood by the people on the coast (rarely used by the Wanyika)
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A forked post, on which the stalks of Guinea-corn are lodged during harvest
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A percentage given out of the profits for breeding goats, sheep, fowls, etc
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The stalk of the banana, when dried and reduced to powder, to mix with snuff
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The stick, or spring, of a trap which is intended to go off on being touched
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To be pressed in the mind; to be depressed, sorrowful; (K.) to pity, to sigh
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.n.]

entries.english: The pit caused by a tumour which was not opened, or by a wound when returning
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Something gathered up, a set of things filed or strung, or stuck upon a stick
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A cocoa-nut tree when very high and slender, with the additional meaning of old
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A bundle of dry grass, tied like a sheaf, generally prepared for thatching a hut
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The eyebrow, the hair being called kumbi, which it is the Wanyika custom to shave
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To feel at ease, to be comfortable, lively, cheerful; to be at liberty or at large
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.n.]

entries.english: A store, anything laid up or provided for future use; provision? From Ku weka, Kij
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Makanda ga nazi, The husks of cocoa-nuts, when on; when off they are called Makumbi
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Makanda ga nazi, The husks of cocoa-nuts, when on; when off they are called Makumbi
entries.context: Rev. W. E. Taylor (1891) Giryama Vocabulary and Collections

entries.english: The name of a kind of beetle, injurious to young cocoa-nut trees; it eats off the top
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Honour; present given in honour of anybody, or in acknowledgment of services rendered
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A pole fixed in the middle of a round hut, and projecting a short distance from the top
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The skin of a goat, when taken by the mfaya from the kambi for the purpose of the ugnaro
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A razor,—a rare instrument among the Wanyika: they shave their heads with a common knife
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To shoot at a venture, fancying by the shaking of the grass that there might be an animal
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.a.]

entries.english: A basin made of clay in the country and unglazed, those imported are called bakuli, a pan
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: N.B.—The word is always pronounced in a high singing tone, the voice resting on the first a
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The lower part of a stem or stalk, corresponding to the kolo in trees, and the sinde in grass
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: To tuck up one's garment at the waist, to give more liberty to the legs in climbing a tree, etc
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: Ni nifuge wariwangu, Give me some milk, that I may stir it into my wari, cooked grain, rice, etc
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.a.]

entries.english: Heads of Guinea-corn, which have fallen to the ground, or such as are not thickly set with grains
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A species of wild aloe; its leaves are shorter than of the konche, but the points are much sharper
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To reply, to join in speech, implying willingness, readiness; when in anger, Udzikisa must be used
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: Kahumania a-ri-ro na-ro, To-day there is a meeting of the elders, but we do not know what it is for
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: That part of the belly under the short ribs, called the hypochondria; the middle of the hypochondria
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To cause to go further, to protract, to prolong, to continue doing anything, to be long in continuance
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.c.]

entries.english: To surpass in strength, to prevail over, prevail upon; to get the better of, to overpower, to overcome
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: The open cloth put round the body and tucked in at the bosom, according to the fashion of Suahili women
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A kind of small pumpkin, peculiar for the excrescences with which it is dotted over; a vegetable marrow
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Any stick when pointed for digging or for ripping up the husk of a cocoa-nut, in order to get out the nut
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Beer, made in various ways, sometimes from millet, sometimes from bananas, when it must be more like cider
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: The skin in which the grain of Guinea-corn is enclosed, and which comes off on the masuche being beaten out
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A pendant from the ear, consisting of a piece of brass, about the length of a finger and worked ornamentally
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A measure, that by which the extent, not quantity, of anything is measured, any stick or rod used for measuring
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Iron; also the dross of iron when reduced to powder and applied, as medicine, to a kind of boils called firangi
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Something knocking or being knocked about; from Ki and Omba, which, in Kns., means to knock, and, in Kij., to beg
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The name of a species of snake, of a shining black colour and with very red eyes, said to be exceedingly venomous
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To break off or asunder, as a thread or string, etc.; but to break to pieces is Ku funsa, to crack or stretch the fingers
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.a.]

entries.english: A very small stool, cut out of one piece of wood; any kind of stool, a chair—a chair as seen with the Mohammedans on the coast
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: Uira wa kiganga, A magic dance; or, A dance instituted by an mganga for a sick person supposed to be possessed by an evil spirit
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [adj.]

entries.english: A sort of enclosed platform, or rack, erected in native huts over the place they make their fire, and which serves as their granary
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A party of men called together for expediting some work in behalf of one of them, as cultivating a piece of ground or building a hut
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The name of a special charm, supposed to have the property of sending those into a deep sleep whom its possessor intends robbing; lit
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: A banjo with one string, made of a small calabash or mauyu, by cutting off the top and bottom and covering the bottom with a piece of skin
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: A kind of basket or bag, with a wide bottom and narrow mouth, made by boys to conceal their little articles of food when they are out of doors
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: It has been superseded by the madzango, and, on account of its great weight, was gladly given up when brass wire found its way to their country
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: An area, a place cleared and levelled to build upon, or for beating out Caffre-corn (muhama); any free and open space suitable for dancing and playing
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: Radically, something laid over or across, both by way of covering and fastening together; also one thing used for keeping and drawing another to itself
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: To stay away, to remain absent, by being fascinated with the conversation of the people you have gone to, or being pleased with the country to which you have gone
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: To look reddish like sound flesh; said of a wound when beginning to heal, to look brown or yellow as fruits, etc., when ripening; also used of meat when being roasted
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: A small wickerwork holder, in form resembling the half of a pair of scales, hung up in the cottage for receiving a pot with ready-cooked food until the time of eating; now rarely used
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [n.]

entries.english: The individual concerned wears for a few days a crown made of clay, but highly decorated, and, as the completion of the honours bestowed on him, receives on his right arm the lumfo, which he wears ever afterwards
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [v.n.]

entries.english: The name of a species of creeper (lubugu), the leaves of which are glutinous, and, being pounded, are used for stopping up cracks in pots, as also for softening the ground when it is too hard for digging, in which case the leaves are beaten into the hole intended to be dug
entries.context: Rev. Dr. L. Krapf & Rev. J. Rebmann, A Nika-English Dictionary (SPCK London, 1887 — Public Domain)

entries.english: A club, made of heavy wood
entries.context: Krapf, Rebmann & Sparshott (1887, pp. 259, 338 s.v. M'oro & Rungu: a village without mumfiria, m'oro, and rungu is merely a mudzi, not a kaya)
Krapf & Rebmann (1887, p. 9 s.v. Avu): In traditional Mijikenda matrilineal (fugo / lukolo) kinship, the maternal uncle (avu) exercised authority over his sister's children (muhua, pl. ahua).

Krapf & Rebmann (1887, p. 346 s.v. Siki): Pounded from sorghum flour (unga wa muhama), red pepper (pilipili), kilungakuku herb, palm-wine dregs (muniu zira za uchi), and lemon (ndimu) or makabu fruit.

entries.english: An oath, connected with charms; an ordeal
entries.translation: kiravo (cha, pl. viravo: mundu, sindano, chungu cha moho, mbare, luemba)
entries.context: Krapf, Rebmann & Sparshott (1887, pp. 180–181 s.v. Kiravo: red-hot hatchet on tongue, hot needle through lips, stone in boiling pot, poisoned food, or dry meal)

entries.english: Not (with verb, as prefix, infix, or suffix)
entries.context: 16. Nika (Giryama / Duruma / Digo) — Sir H. H. Johnston, Comparative Study of the Bantu Languages (1919, Vol. I, pp. 98–110)

entries.english: Nephew or niece (a man's sister's son or daughter)
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887, p. 276 s.v. Muhua): Hiyu ni muhua wangu, muana wa mumbuyangu (This is my nephew/niece, my sister's child).
Krapf & Rebmann (1887, p. 390 s.v. Yoyo): Yoyo, mugeni! Yoyo mulumangu! udzihenda to kudza na afia. Yoyo baba! Yoyo nduguyangu!

entries.english: For God so loved the world (John 3:16 specimen in Giryama)
entries.translation: Kwani Mulungu arizhahendza at'u a ulimwengu hata akimupa Mwanawe waeri
entries.context: The Gospel in Many Tongues (BFBS, London, 1921, p. 47 — Giryama)

entries.english: Communal rain-making charm and three-day ritual restriction (muhondo)
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887, p. 352 s.v. Sosonga): Villagers gather food for two days because on the third day (muhondo) no one may go to the fields; they drag a skin (kichingo) and perform the sosonga rain rite.

entries.english: The name of a town and tribe of Wanyika, one day's journey north of Rabai
entries.context: Krapf & Rebmann (1887) Nika-English Dictionary [adj.]

entries.english: The name given to the rites and ceremonies the young women have to pass through on their promotion from the gniere to the kambi state, exactly answering to the ugnaro of the young men
entries.context: Krapf, Rebmann & Sparshott (1887, p. 115 s.v. Gundi)
